newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian rebels will not blow hole in economy.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian rebels will not blow hole in economy.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas' spectacular takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima has wounded investor confidence but is unlikely to shatter Peru's emerging economy, analysts say.

In the immediate aftermath of the Dec. 17 storming of the compound, many predicted a disastrous impact on the economy, with a resurgence of political violence derailing free-market reforms and scaring away foreign investors.
But as the dust has settled and the siege dragged on, early gloom over the implications for the economy has given way to quiet confidence among analysts that the impact will in the end be limited.
"In the first moments after the attack, I thought it was going to be catastrophic," said Oscar Jasaui, president of the Lima chamber of economists.

"But after some days, I began to think that this is just an isolated event and that the world has taken it like that. It has no wider meaning than a group of terrorists attacking the home of the ambassador."
That shift in opinion was echoed at the Lima Stock Exchange, normally a reliable bellwether of economic mood.

Its blue-chip index plunged 4.43 percent as investors panicked the morning after the takeover, forcing a suspension of trading by midday. But shares began to rise two days later and continued gaining to close on Friday above pre-crisis levels.
"It seems that investors have already taken this event by the horns and everything has returned to normal," said Eduardo Maradieque, head of economic studies at local brokerage MGS.
No one doubts, however, that some fallout is inevitable.

"It seems to me that the most direct impact will be on Japanese investment," said William Romary, senior economist for Latin America at UBS Securities. "There had been a lot of talk in Japan about investing in Peru. But now they will be asking 'Are we making these decisions carefully?'"

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas deliberately chose the Japanese ambassador's home as their target to show disgust at Tokyo's enthusiastic support for Fujimori and his six-year-old economic reform program. After releasing more than 400 hostages, the rebels still held 83 on Sunday, including Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
But while Japanese companies may think twice about coming to, or staying in, Peru, it was business as usual for some other firms.

Six days after the hostage crisis began, U.S. telecommunications company BellSouth Corp confirmed its offer to buy 54 to 64 percent of Peruvian cellular phone company Tele 2000. A 54 percent stake would cost $100 million.
Such an endorsement of Peru's investment possibilities was a vital boost to the government.
Even amid the initial panic, some investment houses ironically gave Peru a thumbs-up as a buy opportunity specifically due to the crisis.

The "attack is only a specific incident and does not represent a new outbreak of violence. We see the (initial) negative reaction of the (stock) market as a good opportunity to buy," said Lima-based Santander Investment, for example, the day after the attack.
Not all were seeing light in the darkness, however.

Bear, Stearns & Co said it would reduce its original 4.0 percent growth forecast for 1997. "Peru had started a mild recovery at the time of the attack. We think this will be put on hold," it said in a report.
And analysts warned that the government, which had been widely lauded from abroad for its investor-friendly policies, now faced a harder battle to maintain its image.

"People had been talking so much about the success story in Peru, but I think this will definitely cause people to take a step back and pause," said Romary. "I don't think it will have a major impact in putting the brakes on investment, but it is a sobering reminder that Peru is a risky place. However, there are still a lot of attractive possibilities."
The government will be keen to refocus attention quickly on those possibilities -- particularly its dynamic privatization program which is the corner-stone of Fujimori's reforms.

Privatization officials said although the siege may temporarily delay some of the auctions planned for early 1997, it should not hold up for long the piecemeal selloff of its oil, fishing, electricity and mining assets.

"The value of what we are selling is not affected by the crazy action of a band of criminals, and the international companies interested know that very well," said one privatization official, who asked not to be named.

Neither is the political crisis expected to force the government to change the direction of its economic program -- now in its sixth year and entering what the government calls a consolidatory "second stage."
The MRTA siege has thrown light once again on Peru's deep-rooted social problems, but the government was already devoting increased resources to this area, analysts agreed.
And the gentle recovery expected for 1997 after this year's slowdown -- itself a reaction to the high growth of previous years -- is not expected to be knocked off course.

"Is this going to change the fundamental paradigm in Peru? Is this a major threat to the government?" said Gary Evans, senior strategist at Lehman Brothers in New York. "The jury is still out, but I don't think so."
